payload.user_instructions:
# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Use the MOOSE conda environment (`conda activate moose`)
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
- Use `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` to validate before committing
- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files
- Write parameter values in the units the reference source used; use the MOOSE units system for conversion — the units system is self-documenting and does not require inline comments
- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable
- Before committing, copy the current session's `.jsonl` file into `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/`. For Claude Code sessions the file is the most recently modified `.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/`; for Codex sessions check the equivalent Codex session directory. Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added
- If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately
- Every commit must reference the associated GitHub issue (e.g. `Refs #<issue-number>` or `Closes #<issue-number>` as appropriate) in the commit message
- **Every commit must include an updated copy of the session `.jsonl`** — before staging, copy the current session file from `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` to `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/` and stage it; this is a critical SQA requirement. Do not remove session files already present in that directory — if multiple Claude/Codex sessions contribute to the same branch and issue, all session files must be kept.
- Every commit must include these trailers:
```
Refs #<issue-number>
AI-assisted: true
AI-model: <model name>
AI-version: <model version>
Co-Authored-By: <model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

## Pull requests
- If the linked issue already contains a complete Reason/Design/Impact description, the PR body should contain only the closing reference (e.g. `Closes #<issue-number>`) — do not duplicate the issue content or leave template sections empty
- If the PR introduces physics/modeling decisions, non-obvious AI reasoning, or tests not described in the issue, add those as a short addendum below the issue reference
- Never merge autonomously

## Never do
- Modify existing passing tests without explicit user instruction
- Modify the build system without explicit user instruction
- Make physics modeling decisions without flagging them to the user
- Suppress or bypass test failures


## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and file path so you can open the source for full instructions when using a specific skill.
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when users want to create a new skill (or update an existing skill) that extends Codex's capabilities with specialized knowledge, workflows, or tool integrations. (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-creator/SKILL.md)

Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
### How to use skills
- Discovery: The list above is the skills available in this session (name + description + file path). Skill bodies live on disk at the listed paths.
- Trigger rules: If the user names a skill (with `$SkillName` or plain text) OR the task clearly matches a skill's description shown above, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.
- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.

  1) After deciding to use a skill, open its `SKILL.md`. Read only enough to follow the workflow.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references relative paths (e.g., `scripts/foo.py`), resolve them relative to the skill directory listed above first, and only consider other paths if needed.

import os
import tempfile

os.environ.setdefault("MPLCONFIGDIR", tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="matplotlib-val-2k-"))

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Changes working directory to script directory for consistent MooseDocs usage.
script_folder = os.path.dirname(__file__)
os.chdir(script_folder)


def get_repo_relative_path(test_path):
    if "/tmap8/doc/" in script_folder.lower():
        return os.path.join("../../../../test/tests/val-2k", test_path)
    return os.path.join(".", test_path)


simulation_csv = get_repo_relative_path("gold/val-2k_out.csv")
experiment_csv = get_repo_relative_path("gold/experiment_data_natural_oxide_fig6.csv")

simulation_data = pd.read_csv(simulation_csv)
time_s = simulation_data["time"]
temperature_k = 300.0 + (3.0 / 60.0) * time_s
release_flux = (
    simulation_data["scaled_flux_surface_left"] + simulation_data["scaled_flux_surface_right"]
)

experiment_data = pd.read_csv(experiment_csv)
has_experiment = not experiment_data.empty

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
ax.plot(
    temperature_k,
    release_flux,
    linestyle="-",
    color="tab:blue",
    label="TMAP8 iteration 1",
)

if has_experiment:
    experiment_temperature = experiment_data["temperature (K)"]
    experiment_flux = experiment_data["release flux (D atoms/m^2/s)"]
    ax.plot(
        experiment_temperature,
        experiment_flux,
        linestyle="--",
        color="k",
        label="Experimental data",
    )

    simulated_on_experiment_grid = np.interp(experiment_temperature, temperature_k, release_flux)
    rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((simulated_on_experiment_grid - experiment_flux) ** 2))
    rmspe = rmse * 100.0 / np.mean(experiment_flux)
    ax.text(700, 0.85 * max(release_flux.max(), experiment_flux.max()), f"RMSPE = {rmspe:.2f} %")
else:
    ax.text(
        520,
        0.85 * release_flux.max(),
        "Experimental CSV pending digitization",
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (K)")
ax.set_ylabel("Release flux (D atoms/m$^2$/s)")
ax.set_xlim(300, 1000)
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.grid(visible=True, which="major", color="0.65", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(loc="best")
ax.minorticks_on()

plt.savefig("val-2k_natural_oxide_iteration_1_comparison.png", bbox_inches="tight", dpi=300)
plt.close(fig)

# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Use the MOOSE conda environment (`conda activate moose`)
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
- Use `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` to validate before committing
- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files
- Write parameter values in the units the reference source used; use the MOOSE units system for conversion — the units system is self-documenting and does not require inline comments
- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable
- Before committing, copy the current session's `.jsonl` file into `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/`. For Claude Code sessions the file is the most recently modified `.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/`; for Codex sessions check the equivalent Codex session directory. Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added

- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns

- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax

- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files

- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable

Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added
- If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately
- Every commit must reference the associated GitHub issue (e.g. `Refs #<issue-number>` or `Closes #<issue-number>` as appropriate) in the commit message
- **Every commit must include an updated copy of the session `.jsonl`** — before staging, copy the current session file from `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` to `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/` and stage it; this is a critical SQA requirement. Do not remove session files already present in that directory — if multiple Claude/Codex sessions contribute to the same branch and issue, all session files must be kept.

```
Refs #<issue-number>
AI-assisted: true
AI-model: <model name>
AI-version: <model version>
Co-Authored-By: <model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

## Pull requests
- If the linked issue already contains a complete Reason/Design/Impact description, the PR body should contain only the closing reference (e.g. `Closes #<issue-number>`) — do not duplicate the issue content or leave template sections empty
- If the PR introduces physics/modeling decisions, non-obvious AI reasoning, or tests not described in the issue, add those as a short addendum below the issue reference
- Never merge autonomously

- Modify existing passing tests without explicit user instruction
- Modify the build system without explicit user instruction
- Make physics modeling decisions without flagging them to the user
- Suppress or bypass test failures

# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Use the MOOSE conda environment (`conda activate moose`)
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
- Use `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` to validate before committing
- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files
- Write parameter values in the units the reference source used; use the MOOSE units system for conversion — the units system is self-documenting and does not require inline comments
- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable
- Before committing, copy the current session's `.jsonl` file into `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/`. For Claude Code sessions the file is the most recently modified `.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/`; for Codex sessions check the equivalent Codex session directory. Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added
- If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately
- Every commit must reference the associated GitHub issue (e.g. `Refs #<issue-number>` or `Closes #<issue-number>` as appropriate) in the commit message
- **Every commit must include an updated copy of the session `.jsonl`** — before staging, copy the current session file from `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` to `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/` and stage it; this is a critical SQA requirement. Do not remove session files already present in that directory — if multiple Claude/Codex sessions contribute to the same branch and issue, all session files must be kept.
- Every commit must include these trailers:
```
Refs #<issue-number>
AI-assisted: true
AI-model: <model name>
AI-version: <model version>
Co-Authored-By: <model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

## Pull requests
- If the linked issue already contains a complete Reason/Design/Impact description, the PR body should contain only the closing reference (e.g. `Closes #<issue-number>`) — do not duplicate the issue content or leave template sections empty
- If the PR introduces physics/modeling decisions, non-obvious AI reasoning, or tests not described in the issue, add those as a short addendum below the issue reference
- Never merge autonomously

## Never do
- Modify existing passing tests without explicit user instruction
- Modify the build system without explicit user instruction
- Make physics modeling decisions without flagging them to the user
- Suppress or bypass test failures

import numpy as np

import matplotlib

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.interpolate import interp1d
from pathlib import Path

img = np.array(Image.open('/tmp/fig6_hi/fig6_plot_only.png').convert('RGB'))
plot = img[127:1279, 278:1708]
inner = plot[3:-3, 3:-3]
H, W, _ = inner.shape

legend = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=bool)
legend[:760, :440] = True

masks = {
    'blue': (inner[:, :, 2] > 150) & (inner[:, :, 0] < 120) & (inner[:, :, 1] < 170),
    'red': (inner[:, :, 0] > 150) & (inner[:, :, 1] < 145) & (inner[:, :, 2] < 145),
    'green': (inner[:, :, 1] > 80) & (inner[:, :, 0] < 170) & (inner[:, :, 2] < 170) & ((inner[:, :, 1] - inner[:, :, 0]) > 8),
    'black': (inner.max(axis=2) < 95),
}
for key in masks:
    masks[key] &= ~legend
    masks[key][:10, :] = False
    masks[key][-10:, :] = False
    masks[key][:, :10] = False
    masks[key][:, -10:] = False

# Remove the grey temperature ramp from the black mask
xs = np.arange(W)
y_temp_guess = np.where(xs < 1375, 1110 - 0.71 * xs, 134)
for i, y in enumerate(y_temp_guess.astype(int)):
    y0 = max(0, y - 24)
    y1 = min(H, y + 24)
    masks['black'][y0:y1, i] = False


def column_groups(mask):
    groups = []
    for i in range(mask.shape[1]):
        ys = np.where(mask[:, i])[0]
        clusters = []
        if ys.size:
            start = ys[0]
            prev = ys[0]
            for y in ys[1:]:
                if y <= prev + 2:
                    prev = y
                else:
                    clusters.append((start + prev) / 2.0)
                    start = y
                    prev = y
            clusters.append((start + prev) / 2.0)
        groups.append(np.array(clusters, dtype=float))
    return groups


def track_curve(groups, x_start, choose='top', max_jump=30.0):
    y = np.full(len(groups), np.nan)
    prev = None
    started = False
    for i in range(len(groups)):
        cand = groups[i]
        if cand.size == 0:
            continue
        if not started:
            if i < x_start:
                continue
            prev = np.min(cand) if choose == 'top' else np.max(cand)
            y[i] = prev
            started = True
            continue
        idx = np.argmin(np.abs(cand - prev))
        if np.abs(cand[idx] - prev) <= max_jump:

def track_curve(groups, x_start, choose='top', max_jump=30.0):
    y = np.full(len(groups), np.nan)
    prev = None
    started = False
    for i in range(len(groups)):
        cand = groups[i]
        if cand.size == 0:
            continue
        if not started:
            if i < x_start:

            prev = np.min(cand) if choose == 'top' else np.max(cand)

def fill_series(series, pre_value=1150.5):

import numpy as np

def get_repo_relative_path(test_path):
    if "/tmap8/doc/" in script_folder.lower():
        return os.path.join("../../../../test/tests/val-2k", test_path)
    return os.path.join(".", test_path)


def get_latest_profile_csv(pattern):
    matches = sorted(glob(pattern))
    if not matches:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No profile CSV found matching {pattern}")
    return matches[-1]


def get_numeric_parameter(parameter_name):
    parameters_file = get_repo_relative_path("parameters_val-2k.params")
    with open(parameters_file, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            stripped = line.strip()
            if stripped.startswith(f"{parameter_name} ="):
                return float(stripped.split("=", maxsplit=1)[1].strip().strip("'"))
    raise KeyError(f"Could not find parameter {parameter_name} in {parameters_file}")

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

gold = Path('test/tests/val-2k/gold')
sample_area_m2 = 10e-3 * 14e-3
for path in sorted(gold.glob('experimental_*.csv')):
    df = pd.read_csv(path, header=None, names=['time_h', 'release_1e13_D_per_s'])
    temperature_k = np.minimum(300.0 + 180.0 * df['time_h'], 1000.0)
    release_flux = df['release_1e13_D_per_s'] * 1e13 / sample_area_m2
    out = pd.DataFrame({
        'temperature (K)': temperature_k,
        'release flux (D atoms/m^2/s)': release_flux,
    })
    out.to_csv(path, index=False)
    print(path.name, len(out))

payload.user_instructions:
# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Use the MOOSE conda environment (`conda activate moose`)
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
- Use `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` to validate before committing
- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files
- Write parameter values in the units the reference source used; use the MOOSE units system for conversion — the units system is self-documenting and does not require inline comments
- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable
- Before committing, copy the current session's `.jsonl` file into `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/`. For Claude Code sessions the file is the most recently modified `.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/`; for Codex sessions check the equivalent Codex session directory. Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added
- If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately
- Every commit must reference the associated GitHub issue (e.g. `Refs #<issue-number>` or `Closes #<issue-number>` as appropriate) in the commit message
- **Every commit must include an updated copy of the session `.jsonl`** — before staging, copy the current session file from `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` to `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/` and stage it; this is a critical SQA requirement. Do not remove session files already present in that directory — if multiple Claude/Codex sessions contribute to the same branch and issue, all session files must be kept.
- Every commit must include these trailers:
```
Refs #<issue-number>
AI-assisted: true
AI-model: <model name>
AI-version: <model version>
Co-Authored-By: <model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

## Pull requests
- If the linked issue already contains a complete Reason/Design/Impact description, the PR body should contain only the closing reference (e.g. `Closes #<issue-number>`) — do not duplicate the issue content or leave template sections empty
- If the PR introduces physics/modeling decisions, non-obvious AI reasoning, or tests not described in the issue, add those as a short addendum below the issue reference
- Never merge autonomously

## Never do
- Modify existing passing tests without explicit user instruction
- Modify the build system without explicit user instruction
- Make physics modeling decisions without flagging them to the user
- Suppress or bypass test failures


## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and file path so you can open the source for full instructions when using a specific skill.
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when users want to create a new skill (or update an existing skill) that extends Codex's capabilities with specialized knowledge, workflows, or tool integrations. (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
### How to use skills
- Discovery: The list above is the skills available in this session (name + description + file path). Skill bodies live on disk at the listed paths.
- Trigger rules: If the user names a skill (with `$SkillName` or plain text) OR the task clearly matches a skill's description shown above, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.
- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.
- How to use a skill (progressive disclosure):
  1) After deciding to use a skill, open its `SKILL.md`. Read only enough to follow the workflow.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references relative paths (e.g., `scripts/foo.py`), resolve them relative to the skill directory listed above first, and only consider other paths if needed.
  3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, load only the specific files needed for the request; don't bulk-load everything.
  4) If `scripts/` exist, prefer running or patching them instead of retyping large code blocks.
  5) If `assets/` or templates exist, reuse them instead of recreating from scratch.
- Coordination and sequencing:
  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skill(s) you're using and why (one short line). If you skip an obvious skill, say why.
- Context hygiene:
  - Keep context small: summarize long sections instead of pasting them; only load extra files when needed.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer opening only files directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless you're blocked.
  - When variants exist (frameworks, providers, domains), pick only the relevant reference file(s) and note that choice.
- Safety and fallback: If a skill can't be applied cleanly (missing files, unclear instructions), state the issue, pick the next-best approach, and continue.

payload.message:
Not as the TDS exposed area.

What the paper supports from [1-s2.0-S2352179122000242-main.pdf](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/1-s2.0-S2352179122000242-main.pdf):
- sample size: `15 × 11.8 × 0.8 mm^3`
- during self-ion damage, a mask with an `opening of 10 × 14 mm` is used
- that mask “leaves an undamaged rim”
- in TDS, the setup “does not need a sample holder,” so the sample sits in a quartz tube

So `10 × 14 mm` is directly justified as the damaged / plasma-loaded front-face area, not as the full area exposed during TDS.

My inference was:
- Fig. 6 reports total release in `D atoms/s`
- if we want an area-normalized quantity, the most defensible local area is the damaged reservoir area, `10 × 14 mm^2`
- that assumes the measured release is dominated by deuterium coming from that damaged front-face region

That inference is reasonable for an effective emitting area, but it is still an inference. It is not stated explicitly in the paper.

The stronger conclusion is:
- for Fig. 6 comparisons, we should stay in the paper’s native units: `time (h)` and `10^13 D atoms/s`
- using `10 × 14 mm^2` to convert to flux should only be done if we document it as an assumed effective damaged-area normalization, not as the literal TDS exposed area

So your correction was right.

# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Use the MOOSE conda environment (`conda activate moose`)
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
- Use `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` to validate before committing
- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files
- Write parameter values in the units the reference source used; use the MOOSE units system for conversion — the units system is self-documenting and does not require inline comments
- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable
- Before committing, copy the current session's `.jsonl` file into `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/`. For Claude Code sessions the file is the most recently modified `.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/`; for Codex sessions check the equivalent Codex session directory. Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added
- If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately
- Every commit must reference the associated GitHub issue (e.g. `Refs #<issue-number>` or `Closes #<issue-number>` as appropriate) in the commit message
- **Every commit must include an updated copy of the session `.jsonl`** — before staging, copy the current session file from `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` to `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/` and stage it; this is a critical SQA requirement. Do not remove session files already present in that directory — if multiple Claude/Codex sessions contribute to the same branch and issue, all session files must be kept.
- Every commit must include these trailers:
```
Refs #<issue-number>
AI-assisted: true
AI-model: <model name>
AI-version: <model version>
Co-Authored-By: <model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

## Pull requests
- If the linked issue already contains a complete Reason/Design/Impact description, the PR body should contain only the closing reference (e.g. `Closes #<issue-number>`) — do not duplicate the issue content or leave template sections empty
- If the PR introduces physics/modeling decisions, non-obvious AI reasoning, or tests not described in the issue, add those as a short addendum below the issue reference
- Never merge autonomously

## Never do
- Modify existing passing tests without explicit user instruction
- Modify the build system without explicit user instruction
- Make physics modeling decisions without flagging them to the user
- Suppress or bypass test failures


## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and file path so you can open the source for full instructions when using a specific skill.
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when users want to create a new skill (or update an existing skill) that extends Codex's capabilities with specialized knowledge, workflows, or tool integrations. (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
### How to use skills
- Discovery: The list above is the skills available in this session (name + description + file path). Skill bodies live on disk at the listed paths.
- Trigger rules: If the user names a skill (with `$SkillName` or plain text) OR the task clearly matches a skill's description shown above, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.
- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.
- How to use a skill (progressive disclosure):
  1) After deciding to use a skill, open its `SKILL.md`. Read only enough to follow the workflow.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references relative paths (e.g., `scripts/foo.py`), resolve them relative to the skill directory listed above first, and only consider other paths if needed.
  3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, load only the specific files needed for the request; don't bulk-load everything.
  4) If `scripts/` exist, prefer running or patching them instead of retyping large code blocks.
  5) If `assets/` or templates exist, reuse them instead of recreating from scratch.
- Coordination and sequencing:
  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skill(s) you're using and why (one short line). If you skip an obvious skill, say why.
- Context hygiene:
  - Keep context small: summarize long sections instead of pasting them; only load extra files when needed.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer opening only files directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless you're blocked.
  - When variants exist (frameworks, providers, domains), pick only the relevant reference file(s) and note that choice.
- Safety and fallback: If a skill can't be applied cleanly (missing files, unclear instructions), state the issue, pick the next-best approach, and continue.

payload.message: Update the model parameters to get a better fit between the TMAP8 predictions and the experimental data. The RMSPE should be lower. To that end, try updating the trapping energies and densities, as well as the diffusivity

I’m going to calibrate the Stage 1 parameters against the natural-oxide `HD + D2` curve, focusing on diffusivity plus the two trap energies and trap densities as you requested. First I’m checking the current `val-2k` parameterization and then I’ll run a small search around it to reduce the RMSPE before I patch the input.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
sim=pd.read_csv('test/tests/val-2k/gold/val-2k_out.csv')
exp=pd.read_csv('test/tests/val-2k/gold/experimental_HD_D2_nat_oxide.csv')
time_h=sim['time']/3600.0
rate=(sim['scaled_flux_surface_left']+sim['scaled_flux_surface_right'])*(10e-3*14e-3)/1e13
interp=np.interp(exp['time (h)'], time_h, rate)
rmspe=np.sqrt(np.mean((interp-exp['release flux (10^13 D atoms/s)'])**2))*100/np.mean(exp['release flux (10^13 D atoms/s)'])
print('current_rmspe',rmspe)
print('sim peak', time_h.iloc[np.argmax(rate)], rate.max())
print('exp peak', exp['time (h)'].iloc[np.argmax(exp['release flux (10^13 D atoms/s)'])], exp['release flux (10^13 D atoms/s)'].max())
PY","workdir":"/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8","yield_time_ms":1000,"max_output_tokens":4000}

Can you read the pdf titled 1-s2.0-S2352179122000242-main.pdf, and then answer the following questions:
	•	Can you explain what the paper is about and what type of experimental data is available?
	•	What kind of physics would you need to capture this experiment? 
	•	If a model is available in the paper, can you explain the model and how it captures the experimental data?
	•	Prepare a /plan to implement this in TMAP8 as a new validation case.

I need the GitHub issue number for this session before I proceed, per the repo instructions. Once you give it, I’ll read the PDF, inspect the relevant TMAP8/MOOSE patterns, and prepare the implementation plan.
issue number: 399

**Paper**
The paper in [1-s2.0-S2352179122000242-main.pdf](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/1-s2.0-S2352179122000242-main.pdf) studies how thin tungsten surface oxides change deuterium release from self-ion-damaged tungsten during TDS.

The experiment builds a deuterium reservoir in a 2.3 micrometer self-damaged W layer, then adds electrochemically grown oxide films from about 5 to 100 nm, plus a natural-oxide reference. The main findings are:
- thicker oxide delays the first TDS peak
- oxide acts as both a transport barrier and a temporary D reservoir
- above about 475 K, released D reacts with the oxide
- above about 700 K, release can be dominated by heavy water until the oxide is consumed

**Available Data**
The paper provides experimental data in plotted form for:
- TDS spectra during a 3 K/min ramp to 1000 K
- species-resolved release: `D2`, `HD`, `HDO`, `D2O`
- oxide-thickness dependence: natural oxide, 5, 10, 15, 25, 50, 100 nm
- NRA D depth profiles before and after oxidation / TDS
- oxygen areal density before and after TDS
- SEM images of oxide morphology before and after heating / TDS
- a 500 K ramp-and-hold experiment for a 100 nm oxide case

I do not see a full raw tabulated dataset in the paper text itself, so for a TMAP8 validation case we should assume the plotted curves will need to be digitized unless supplementary/raw data is found elsewhere.

**Physics Needed**
A minimal model would need:
- 1D diffusion of mobile D in tungsten
- multiple trapping / detrapping populations in self-damaged W
- prescribed temperature history for loading / cooldown / TDS
- an explicit oxide layer, or an effective surface barrier, to delay release

A faithful model of the paper’s main result would additionally need:
- D transport in the oxide
- partitioning / exchange across the W-oxide interface
- oxide oxygen inventory
- reaction of D with oxide oxygen to produce `HDO` / `D2O`
- oxide reduction / depletion so the release channel switches back to `D2` / `HD`
- possibly an effective treatment of channel formation in thick oxides during the 500 K hold

Existing TMAP8 clearly supports the tungsten diffusion/trapping baseline via [val-2d.md](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/doc/content/verification_and_validation/val-2d.md), [val-2f.md](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/doc/content/verification_and_validation/val-2f.md), and [SpeciesTrappingPhysics.md](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/doc/content/source/physics/SpeciesTrappingPhysics.md). A fully mechanistic oxide-reduction / heavy-water model does not appear to be available out of the box from the current physics set I inspected.

**Model In Paper**
The paper does not present a new predictive TDS transport model. It is primarily an experimental study.

What it does use:
- SIMNRA / MultiSIMNRA for oxygen analysis from RBS
- NRADC / NRA deconvolution for D depth profiles
- D-balance calibration to infer absolute heavy-water fluxes from QMS + NRA

So if we implement this in TMAP8, we would be building a new validation model inspired by the experiment, not reproducing an existing model from the paper.

**/plan**
1. Define scope as two stages.
   Stage 1: effective validation case with self-damaged W plus oxide barrier/reservoir, targeting peak shift and total release trends.
   Stage 2: mechanistic extension with oxygen depletion and `HDO` / `D2O` production.

2. Use [val-2f.i](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/test/tests/val-2f/val-2f.i) as the tungsten trapping baseline and [val-2d.i](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/test/tests/val-2d/val-2d.i) as the TDS validation template.

3. Create a new case, likely `val-2h`, with:
- `test/tests/val-2h/val-2h.i`
- `test/tests/val-2h/tests`
- `test/tests/val-2h/comparison_val-2h.py`
- `test/tests/val-2h/gold/` for digitized experimental CSVs
- `doc/content/verification_and_validation/val-2h.md`

4. Build Stage 1 with existing physics:
- 1D W domain plus thin oxide subdomain
- temperature-dependent D diffusion
- multiple W trap populations
- effective oxide diffusivity and optional oxide traps
- compare natural oxide and one thick-oxide case first, preferably 100 nm

5. Validate Stage 1 against:
- first-peak shift with oxide thickness
- total desorption flux shape
- 500 K hold plateau for the thick oxide case, if the effective barrier can reproduce it

6. Decide whether Stage 1 is sufficient.
   If not, add new physics for:
- oxygen inventory variable in oxide
- D + O reaction sink/source terms
- species bookkeeping for `D2` / `HD` vs `HDO` / `D2O`
- oxide depletion feedback on barrier strength

7. Add comparison plots and error metrics per V&V standards in [verification_and_validation_standards.md](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/doc/content/verification_and_validation/verification_and_validation_standards.md).

8. Add light and heavy tests, following the existing pattern in [test/tests/val-2d/tests](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/test/tests/val-2d/tests) and [test/tests/val-2f/tests](/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8/test/tests/val-2f/tests).

My recommendation is to start with Stage 1 and explicitly state in the documentation that it is an effective barrier/reservoir model, not yet a mechanistic oxide-reduction / water-formation model. If you want, I can turn this into a concrete implementation design for `val-2h` next.
I have several comments about this plan:
Go ahead. If the comments affect scope, physics fidelity, or whether this should be an effective vs mechanistic validation case, I’ll fold them into a revised plan.

1. the validation case name would be val-2k based on other validation cases being currently added. 2. I want the plan to involved more step to be able to incrementally increase the complexity of the model over time. This will help understand each new piece of he model as it's being added based on comparison against the exeprimental data. As a result, I want to focus first on the naturally oxidized experiment and develop a simplified model with diffusion, surface reactions, and trapping for this case alone. First, teh model should only account for D and D2, and a following iteration should include hydrogen and water species. Then, expand to the cases with an oxide layer, in particular the results of Fig. 6 with natural oxide, and an oxide layer thickness of 5 nm, 10 nm, and 15 nm. Note also that the data from fig. 5 with the 100 nm thick oxide layer is not quantitative and is more challenging to use for validation, so I prefer not to use it for now. Note also that each iteration should be compared to experimental data to see the progression as the model evolves. 3. I agree with the part of the plan that aims to treat the oxide layer as a constant layer, and only after expand to model the oxide reduction happening as the releasing deuterium reduces the oxide.

**Revised /plan for `val-2k`**

1. Define `val-2k` as an incremental validation campaign, not a single final model.
   Each increment should produce a runnable TMAP8 case, a comparison plot against the paper’s experimental data, and a short note on what new physics was added and what mismatch remains.

2. Start with the natural-oxide experiment only.
   Ignore the thick artificial oxide cases at first so the baseline physics is easier to interpret.

3. Iteration 1: natural oxide, `D` in W with trapping, release only as `D2`.
   Physics:
   - 1D D diffusion in tungsten
   - multiple trapping / detrapping populations in self-damaged W
   - vacuum-side surface recombination to `D2`
   - prescribed thermal history matching the experiment
   Validation target:
   - total non-oxygen-bearing release for the natural oxide case
   Goal:
   - establish the tungsten diffusion/trapping baseline before adding oxide chemistry

4. Iteration 2: natural oxide, add explicit surface reaction pathways involving hydrogen and water species, but still without an explicit oxide subdomain.
   Physics:
   - keep Iteration 1 baseline
   - add H-containing surface chemistry needed to represent `HD`, `HDO`, and `D2O` release channels in an effective surface model
   Validation target:
   - natural oxide data from the species-resolved release curves
   Goal:
   - understand how much of the natural-oxide behavior can be captured with surface chemistry alone

5. Iteration 3: introduce a constant oxide layer for the natural-oxide case.
   Physics:
   - add a fixed thin oxide layer as a separate transport region
   - keep oxide properties constant in time
   - no oxide reduction yet
   Validation target:
   - natural oxide case again
   Goal:
   - separate barrier/reservoir effects from chemistry effects

6. Iteration 4: extend the constant-oxide-layer model to artificial oxide thicknesses of 5 nm, 10 nm, and 15 nm.
   Focus on Fig. 6 comparisons only:
   - natural oxide
   - 5 nm
   - 10 nm
   - 15 nm
   Physics:
   - same as Iteration 3
   - vary only oxide thickness first, then calibrate oxide transport / trapping / interfacial parameters if needed
   Goal:
   - check whether a fixed oxide layer can reproduce the trend in peak shifts and species partitioning

7. Iteration 5: assess whether constant-oxide physics is sufficient.
   Compare all four cases side by side and document:
   - what is captured
   - where the model systematically fails
   - whether failures point to missing oxide depletion / reduction physics

8. Iteration 6: add oxide reduction as a moving-evolution effect only after the constant-layer model is understood.
   Physics to add later:
   - oxygen inventory in the oxide
   - D-driven oxide consumption
   - feedback of oxide depletion on transport and release products
   This stage is deferred until the fixed-layer model is validated as far as possible.

9. Exclude the 100 nm Fig. 5 case from the initial validation scope.
   Use it only later, if needed, as a qualitative check, not as the primary quantitative target.

10. For each iteration, deliver the same artifacts:
   - one or more TMAP8 input files
   - experimental CSV data used for comparison
   - `comparison_val-2k.py`
   - updated `val-2k.md`
   - test coverage with light/heavy runs as appropriate

This gives a cleaner progression:
- tungsten diffusion/trapping
- effective surface chemistry
- constant oxide layer
- oxide-thickness study
- oxide reduction later

If you want, I can next turn this into a more concrete implementation sequence mapped to likely TMAP8 objects and expected new code vs reusable existing code.

This is now a better plan that can be further refined  as we progress. Note, however, that rather than create new TMAP8 input files and .py files at every step, I want you, as much as possible, to update them or expand input files using the !include feature.

Understood. I’ll treat `val-2k` as an evolving validation case and avoid creating parallel input / plotting files unless there is a clear technical reason.

I’ll structure it so the same core files grow over time:
- a main `val-2k.i`
- included fragments for incremental physics using `!include`
- a single `comparison_val-2k.py` expanded as new experimental comparisons are added
- one `val-2k.md` updated as each iteration is completed

Where useful, I’ll split the input into reusable pieces such as:
- temperature history
- tungsten diffusion / trapping baseline
- natural-oxide surface reactions
- explicit oxide-layer blocks
- later oxide-reduction additions

That should keep the model history readable while still letting each iteration be compared against experiment in a controlled way.
great plan
Next step is to start from the natural-oxide case and define the initial `val-2k` file structure so later iterations can be added with `!include` blocks instead of branching into separate inputs.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
sim = pd.read_csv('test/tests/val-2k/gold/val-2k_out.csv')
exp = pd.read_csv('test/tests/val-2k/gold/experimental_HD_D2_nat_oxide.csv')
time_h = sim['time'].to_numpy()/3600.0
release = (sim['scaled_flux_surface_left'].to_numpy()+sim['scaled_flux_surface_right'].to_numpy())*(10e-3*14e-3)/1e13
exp_t = exp.iloc[:,0].to_numpy()
exp_y = exp.iloc[:,1].to_numpy()
sim_i = np.interp(exp_t, time_h, release)
mask = np.abs(exp_y) > 1e-12
rmspe = np.sqrt(np.mean(((sim_i[mask]-exp_y[mask])/exp_y[mask])**2))*100
print('baseline_rmspe', rmspe)
print('sim_peak_time_h', time_h[np.argmax(release)])
print('sim_peak', release.max())
print('exp_peak_time_h', exp_t[np.argmax(exp_y)])
print('exp_peak', exp_y.max())

- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change

import math, os, pathlib, re, shutil, subprocess, sys
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

root = pathlib.Path('/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8')
src = root / 'test/tests/val-2k'
outdir = pathlib.Path('/tmp/val2k_sweep')
work = outdir / 'work'
if outdir.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(outdir)
outdir.mkdir(parents=True)
shutil.copytree(src, work)

param_path = work / 'parameters_val-2k.params'
base = param_path.read_text()
exp = pd.read_csv(root / 'test/tests/val-2k/gold/experimental_HD_D2_nat_oxide.csv')
exp_t = exp.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy()
exp_y = exp.iloc[:, 1].to_numpy()
mask = np.abs(exp_y) > 1e-12
sample_area_m2 = 10e-3 * 14e-3

patterns = {
    'D0': r"diffusion_W_preexponential = '\$\{units [^\n]+ m\^2/s -> mum\^2/s\}'",
    'ED': r"diffusion_W_energy = '\$\{units [^\n]+ eV\}'",
    'E1': r"detrapping_energy_1 = '\$\{fparse \$\{units [^\n]+ eV -> J\} / kb\}'",
    'E2': r"detrapping_energy_2 = '\$\{fparse \$\{units [^\n]+ eV -> J\} / kb\}'",
    'C1': r"trap_site_fraction_1 = [^\n]+",
    'C2': r"trap_site_fraction_2 = [^\n]+",
}

candidates = [
    (0, 1.6e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.020, 0.015),
    (1, 1.6e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.018, 0.012),
    (2, 1.6e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.015, 0.010),
    (3, 2.0e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.018, 0.012),
    (4, 2.0e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.015, 0.010),
    (5, 2.0e-7, 0.28, 1.14, 1.63, 0.018, 0.012),
    (6, 2.0e-7, 0.28, 1.14, 1.63, 0.015, 0.010),
    (7, 1.8e-7, 0.28, 1.14, 1.63, 0.017, 0.011),
    (8, 1.9e-7, 0.285, 1.15, 1.65, 0.015, 0.010),
    (9, 1.8e-7, 0.29, 1.16, 1.68, 0.015, 0.010),
]

results = []
curves = []
for idx, D0, ED, E1, E2, C1, C2 in candidates:
    text = base
    repls = {
        'D0': f"diffusion_W_preexponential = '${{units {D0:g} m^2/s -> mum^2/s}}'",
        'ED': f"diffusion_W_energy = '${{units {ED:g} eV}}'",
        'E1': f"detrapping_energy_1 = '${{fparse ${{units {E1:g} eV -> J}} / kb}}'",
        'E2': f"detrapping_energy_2 = '${{fparse ${{units {E2:g} eV -> J}} / kb}}'",
        'C1': f"trap_site_fraction_1 = {C1}",
        'C2': f"trap_site_fraction_2 = {C2}",
    }
    for key, pattern in patterns.items():
        text = re.sub(pattern, repls[key], text)
    param_path.write_text(text)
    for path in work.glob('val-2k_out*'):
        path.unlink()
    cmd = f"source ~/miniforge/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && conda activate moose && {root/'tmap8-opt'} -i val-2k.i"
    run = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, cwd=work, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True)
    if run.returncode != 0:
        print(f"candidate {idx}: FAIL")
        print(run.stdout[-3000:])
        sys.stdout.flush()
        continue
    sim = pd.read_csv(work / 'val-2k_out.csv')
    time_h = sim['time'].to_numpy() / 3600.0
    release = (sim['scaled_flux_surface_left'].to_numpy() + sim['scaled_flux_surface_right'].to_numpy()) * sample_area_m2 / 1e13
    sim_interp = np.interp(exp_t, time_h, release)

    peak_idx = int(np.argmax(release))

        'rmspe_percent': rmspe,
        'diffusion_W_preexponential_m2_s': D0,
        'diffusion_W_energy_eV': ED,
        'detrapping_energy_1_eV': E1,
        'detrapping_energy_2_eV': E2,
        'trap_site_fraction_1': C1,
        'trap_site_fraction_2': C2,
        'peak_time_h': peak_t,
        'peak_release_1e13_D_s': peak_y,
    })
    curves.append((idx, time_h, release, peak_t, peak_y, rmspe))
    print(f"candidate {idx}: RMSPE={rmspe:.3f}% peak_t={peak_t:.3f} h peak={peak_y:.3f} x1e13 D/s")
    sys.stdout.flush()

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values('candidate')
results_path = outdir / 'val-2k_sweep_summary.csv'
results_df.to_csv(results_path, index=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 7))
ax.plot(exp_t, exp_y, color='black', linewidth=2.5, marker='o', markersize=3, label='Experimental natural oxide')
colors = plt.cm.tab10(np.linspace(0, 1, max(len(curves), 1)))
for color, (idx, time_h, release, peak_t, peak_y, rmspe) in zip(colors, curves):

ax.set_xlabel('Time (h)')
ax.set_ylabel('Release flux (10^13 D atoms/s)')
ax.set_title('val-2k natural-oxide sweep against Fig. 6 data')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
ax.set_xlim(left=0)
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plot_path = outdir / 'val-2k_sweep_plot.png'
fig.savefig(plot_path, dpi=200)
print(f"wrote {results_path}")
print(f"wrote {plot_path}")

{"cmd":"source ~/miniforge/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && conda activate moose && python3 -u - <<'PY'
import math, pathlib, re, shutil, subprocess, sys
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

root = pathlib.Path('/Users/simopa/projects/tmap8')
src = root / 'test/tests/val-2k'
outdir = pathlib.Path('/tmp/val2k_sweep_lowD')
work = outdir / 'work'
if outdir.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(outdir)
outdir.mkdir(parents=True)
shutil.copytree(src, work)

param_path = work / 'parameters_val-2k.params'
base = param_path.read_text()
exp = pd.read_csv(root / 'test/tests/val-2k/gold/experimental_HD_D2_nat_oxide.csv')
exp_t = exp.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy()
exp_y = exp.iloc[:, 1].to_numpy()
mask = np.abs(exp_y) > 1e-12
sample_area_m2 = 10e-3 * 14e-3

patterns = {
    'D0': r"diffusion_W_preexponential = '\$\{units [^\n]+ m\^2/s -> mum\^2/s\}'",
    'ED': r"diffusion_W_energy = '\$\{units [^\n]+ eV\}'",
    'E1': r"detrapping_energy_1 = '\$\{fparse \$\{units [^\n]+ eV -> J\} / kb\}'",
    'E2': r"detrapping_energy_2 = '\$\{fparse \$\{units [^\n]+ eV -> J\} / kb\}'",
    'C1': r"trap_site_fraction_1 = [^\n]+",
    'C2': r"trap_site_fraction_2 = [^\n]+",
}

candidates = [
    (0, 1.6e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.020, 0.015),
    (1, 1.4e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.015, 0.010),
    (2, 1.2e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.015, 0.010),
    (3, 1.0e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.015, 0.010),
    (4, 1.2e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.014, 0.009),
    (5, 1.0e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.014, 0.009),
    (6, 8.0e-8, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.014, 0.009),
    (7, 1.2e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.013, 0.008),
    (8, 1.0e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.013, 0.008),
    (9, 8.0e-8, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.013, 0.008),
    (10, 1.2e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.012, 0.007),
    (11, 1.0e-7, 0.28, 1.15, 1.65, 0.012, 0.007),
]

results = []
curves = []
for idx, D0, ED, E1, E2, C1, C2 in candidates:
    text = base
    repls = {
        'D0': f"diffusion_W_preexponential = '${{units {D0:g} m^2/s -> mum^2/s}}'",
        'ED': f"diffusion_W_energy = '${{units {ED:g} eV}}'",
        'E1': f"detrapping_energy_1 = '${{fparse ${{units {E1:g} eV -> J}} / kb}}'",
        'E2': f"detrapping_energy_2 = '${{fparse ${{units {E2:g} eV -> J}} / kb}}'",
        'C1': f"trap_site_fraction_1 = {C1}",
        'C2': f"trap_site_fraction_2 = {C2}",
    }
    for key, pattern in patterns.items():
        text = re.sub(pattern, repls[key], text)
    param_path.write_text(text)
    for path in work.glob('val-2k_out*'):
        path.unlink()
    cmd = f"source ~/miniforge/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && conda activate moose && {root/'tmap8-opt'} -i val-2k.i"
    run = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, cwd=work, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True)
    if run.returncode != 0:
        print(f"candidate {idx}: FAIL")
        print(run.stdout[-3000:])
        sys.stdout.flush()
        continue
    sim = pd.read_csv(work / 'val-2k_out.csv')
    time_h = sim['time'].to_numpy() / 3600.0
    release = (sim['scaled_flux_surface_left'].to_numpy() + sim['scaled_flux_surface_right'].to_numpy()) * sample_area_m2 / 1e13
    sim_interp = np.interp(exp_t, time_h, release)
    rmspe = math.sqrt(np.mean(((sim_interp[mask] - exp_y[mask]) / exp_y[mask]) ** 2)) * 100.0
    peak_idx = int(np.argmax(release))
    peak_t = float(time_h[peak_idx])
    peak_y = float(release[peak_idx])
    results.append({
        'candidate': idx,
        'rmspe_percent': rmspe,
        'diffusion_W_preexponential_m2_s': D0,
        'diffusion_W_energy_eV': ED,
        'detrapping_energy_1_eV': E1,
        'detrapping_energy_2_eV': E2,
        'trap_site_fraction_1': C1,
        'trap_site_fraction_2': C2,
        'peak_time_h': peak_t,
        'peak_release_1e13_D_s': peak_y,
    })
    curves.append((idx, time_h, release, peak_t, peak_y, rmspe))
    print(f"candidate {idx}: RMSPE={rmspe:.3f}% peak_t={peak_t:.3f} h peak={peak_y:.3f} x1e13 D/s")
    sys.stdout.flush()

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values('candidate')
results_path = outdir / 'val-2k_sweep_summary.csv'
results_df.to_csv(results_path, index=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 7))
ax.plot(exp_t, exp_y, color='black', linewidth=2.5, marker='o', markersize=3, label='Experimental natural oxide')
colors = plt.cm.tab20(np.linspace(0, 1, max(len(curves), 1)))
for color, (idx, time_h, release, peak_t, peak_y, rmspe) in zip(colors, curves):
    ax.plot(time_h, release, color=color, linewidth=1.6, alpha=0.9, label=f'{idx}: RMSPE {rmspe:.1f}%')
    ax.text(peak_t, peak_y, str(idx), color=color, fontsize=9, fontweight='bold', ha='left', va='bottom',
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.15', facecolor='white', edgecolor=color, linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.85))
ax.set_xlabel('Time (h)')
ax.set_ylabel('Release flux (10^13 D atoms/s)')
ax.set_title('val-2k low-diffusivity / low-trap-density sweep')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
ax.set_xlim(left=0)
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=8, ncol=2)
fig.tight_layout()
plot_path = outdir / 'val-2k_sweep_plot.png'
fig.savefig(plot_path, dpi=200)
print(f"wrote {results_path}")
print(f"wrote {plot_path}")

payload.user_instructions:
# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Use the MOOSE conda environment (`conda activate moose`)
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
- Use `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` to validate before committing
- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files
- Write parameter values in the units the reference source used; use the MOOSE units system for conversion — the units system is self-documenting and does not require inline comments
- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable
- Before committing, copy the current session's `.jsonl` file into `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/`. For Claude Code sessions the file is the most recently modified `.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/`; for Codex sessions check the equivalent Codex session directory. Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added
- If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately
- Every commit must reference the associated GitHub issue (e.g. `Refs #<issue-number>` or `Closes #<issue-number>` as appropriate) in the commit message
- **Every commit must include an updated copy of the session `.jsonl`** — before staging, copy the current session file from `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` to `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/` and stage it; this is a critical SQA requirement. Do not remove session files already present in that directory — if multiple Claude/Codex sessions contribute to the same branch and issue, all session files must be kept.
- Every commit must include these trailers:
```
Refs #<issue-number>
AI-assisted: true
AI-model: <model name>
AI-version: <model version>
Co-Authored-By: <model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

## Pull requests
- If the linked issue already contains a complete Reason/Design/Impact description, the PR body should contain only the closing reference (e.g. `Closes #<issue-number>`) — do not duplicate the issue content or leave template sections empty
- If the PR introduces physics/modeling decisions, non-obvious AI reasoning, or tests not described in the issue, add those as a short addendum below the issue reference
- Never merge autonomously

## Never do
- Modify existing passing tests without explicit user instruction
- Modify the build system without explicit user instruction
- Make physics modeling decisions without flagging them to the user
- Suppress or bypass test failures


## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and file path so you can open the source for full instructions when using a specific skill.
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when users want to create a new skill (or update an existing skill) that extends Codex's capabilities with specialized knowledge, workflows, or tool integrations. (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: /Users/simopa/.codex/skills/.system/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
### How to use skills
- Discovery: The list above is the skills available in this session (name + description + file path). Skill bodies live on disk at the listed paths.
- Trigger rules: If the user names a skill (with `$SkillName` or plain text) OR the task clearly matches a skill's description shown above, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.
- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.
- How to use a skill (progressive disclosure):
  1) After deciding to use a skill, open its `SKILL.md`. Read only enough to follow the workflow.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references relative paths (e.g., `scripts/foo.py`), resolve them relative to the skill directory listed above first, and only consider other paths if needed.
  3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, load only the specific files needed for the request; don't bulk-load everything.
  4) If `scripts/` exist, prefer running or patching them instead of retyping large code blocks.
  5) If `assets/` or templates exist, reuse them instead of recreating from scratch.
- Coordination and sequencing:
  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skill(s) you're using and why (one short line). If you skip an obvious skill, say why.
- Context hygiene:
  - Keep context small: summarize long sections instead of pasting them; only load extra files when needed.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer opening only files directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless you're blocked.
  - When variants exist (frameworks, providers, domains), pick only the relevant reference file(s) and note that choice.
- Safety and fallback: If a skill can't be applied cleanly (missing files, unclear instructions), state the issue, pick the next-best approach, and continue.
